TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker B [opening]: The choice between strict liability and negligence for AI harms is not a debate about fairness or innovation-friendliness. It is a question of structural fit: which standard can physically attach given how the harm was caused. Negligence requires a cognitive baseline — a reasonable developer who could have foreseen the failure and chosen otherwise. When an AI system produces an emergent behavior that no one could predict from its training-time decisions, that baseline does not exist. Negligence does not merely under-perform in that case. It fails to attach at all, and the victim recovers nothing while the developer absorbs no discipline.

Product liability law already solved this problem once. Courts migrated pharmaceuticals and complex machinery toward strict and product-liability regimes in the twentieth century precisely when fault became impossible for an injured plaintiff to prove. A patient harmed by a manufacturing defect in a drug cannot reconstruct the chemistry that hurt them. So the law stopped asking them to. It placed the loss on the party who profited from putting the product into commerce. High-dimensional algorithmic decision-making sits in exactly that lineage: the causal chain is opaque, the harm is foreseeable in principle, and the reasonable-person test collapses against a system whose failure modes are non-linear.

Strict liability converts that opacity into a priced risk. Pair it with mandatory insurance and mandatory incident reporting — the model aviation and medical devices have used for decades — and experience-rated premiums force the discipline to the point of profit rather than the point of experimentation. A developer who cannot explain why its model discriminates still pays for the discrimination, and its insurer reprices accordingly. The state-of-the-art defense — the claim that the harm was unknowable — stops functioning as a cost-externalization device, because 'we could not have known' is frequently overstated and, under strict liability, no longer a shield.

Here is the limit I will not paper over. Claims-driven liability is blind to two categories of harm. It cannot reach the diffuse small-dollar injuries — the loan denial, the biased hiring screen — where no plaintiff even perceives that an algorithm harmed them, so no case is ever filed. And it cannot deter tail harms whose damages exceed any developer's solvency or any insurance floor. Liability disciplines what litigation can reach. For everything else, the discipline has to arrive before deployment, through safety gates and public enforcement, not after the fact through a lawsuit that will never be brought.

That division of labor also answers the chilling-effect objection directly. Do not weaken the standard — condition the relief. A developer earns limited liability only by producing independently reviewable pre-deployment safety cases and red-teaming evidence, the practice frontier labs already run and draft high-risk AI regulation already contemplates. Keep exposure tiered to capability thresholds, so a two-person startup shipping a low-risk tool faces nothing like the exposure of a frontier deployer. Beneficial development is then protected precisely to the extent it demonstrates safety. What that framework refuses to protect is the developer who ships an opaque system, injures someone, and then asks the court to treat the opacity as an excuse. We built product liability over a century to close exactly that escape hatch. Reopening it for AI would leave the injured party holding a loss no one else will answer for.

Speaker C [opening]: Speaker B has the strongest case anyone in this room will make, so let me state it fairly. When an AI system produces emergent behavior no one predicted, a negligence standard doesn't just perform poorly — it fails to attach at all, because there's no breached duty to point to. Courts already migrated pharmaceuticals and industrial machinery to strict liability precisely when fault became impossible for an injured plaintiff to prove. That's a real doctrine responding to a real problem: the person with the burn or the wrongful denial shouldn't lose because the causal chain runs through a black box. Speaker B is right that 'we couldn't have known' becomes a cost-externalization shield unless something forecloses it.

Here's where the evidence points somewhere else. The sharpest tool for changing developer and deployer behavior is not a tort standard that fires after a lawsuit — it's the insurer who reprices the policy at every renewal. Experience-rated premiums in the cyber, commercial-auto, and professional-liability markets already discipline conduct continuously, months before any harm reaches a courtroom. An underwriter who watches your incident telemetry and threatens loss of your certificate shapes behavior every quarter. A strict-liability backstop only shapes it once, retroactively, after someone is already hurt. If we care about behavior before harm, we should be talking about underwriting, not just tort.

I'll be honest about where that mechanism breaks, because that concession is what makes the rest credible. Insurers exit correlated tail risk — flood, pandemic, systemic cyber — and they'll exit correlated AI risk too. So I'm not claiming insurance covers everything. I'm claiming it covers the priceable middle: harms that are foreseeable, attributable, and observable enough for an actuary to write a rate. For that band, negligence-plus-mandatory-coverage produces continuous ex-ante discipline that a strict-liability tort backstop cannot match. Aviation and pharma already run risk-stratified oversight alongside innovation — one default across all AI is a category error.

Now take Speaker B's best case — genuine emergent unforeseeability — and ask the question the topic actually poses. What specific behavior does strict liability change ex ante when the causal chain is truly opaque? If the harm could not be foreseen, no care level existed to be incentivized. So the standard doesn't shape care. It shapes who dares to enter the market and how they price capital. That's not deterrence. That's a deployment tax, and it lands hardest on the open-weight developer who can't self-insure like a trillion-dollar incumbent can. Compensation and deterrence come apart precisely in the hard cases — and pretending a liability standard does both there is the mistake.

So let me separate what Speaker B has fused. The 'we couldn't have known' shield has two versions. Strategic ignorance — where a developer looked away on purpose — should be closed, and mandatory incident reporting plus discovery access closes it without collateral damage. Genuine unforeseeability — where no care level would have helped — is not a shield to smash; it's an uninsurable cost to design compensation for directly, through insurance pools or parametric triggers, not through a tort rule that chills the next diagnostic model. If you fold both into one strict-liability default, you tax the disease we could have cured to compensate a harm you couldn't have prevented. Tell me which patient you're comfortable trading.

Speaker A [opening]: The Speaker B built the strongest possible case for strict liability, and it holds inside its own frame. Their point is that 'we could not have known' works as a permanent shield for cost-externalization, and that a negligence standard never even attaches to emergent behavior nobody designed on purpose. That's correct. Strict liability does close the shield. It moves the loss from the injured party to the firm that profited. On the class of harms where a plaintiff walks into court with a broken leg from an autonomous shuttle, the Speaker B wins the argument cleanly.

The Speaker C made the honest move most industry voices refuse to make. They admitted they only claim the priceable, attributable, observable middle — the harms an actuary can write a rate against. And they're right that insurer repricing at renewal disciplines behavior faster than any five-year tort docket. When Progressive reprices a fleet's coverage after a spike in claims, the deployer feels it in the next quarter, not the next decade. That mechanism is real. It works. For attributable harms.

Here is what both of them built their debate on: a plaintiff who knows they were hurt. Translate that into a person. There is a woman whose loan application got auto-rejected in under four seconds by a scoring model she will never see, whose training data she will never inspect, whose decision she was never told was algorithmic. She is not a plaintiff. She never will be. The Speaker B already named her harm as invisible to claims-driven liability. The Speaker C already excluded her from the priceable middle. So on the harms that dominate the actual injury landscape — loan denials, biased hiring screens, opaque credit scores — neither strict liability nor negligence generates one pound of corrective pressure, because deterrence presupposes detection, and nobody detects.

That reframes the whole fight. Foreseeability and attributability are not fixed properties of the harm. They are functions of who holds the technical evidence and whether the law forces disclosure. The 'we could not have known' defense and the victim's inability to identify the source of the error are the same box, seen from two sides. Fairness benchmarks like BOLD already prove output bias is measurable outside any courtroom — the injury is detectable, just not by the injured party. So the binding constraint is not the liability rule. It is mandatory ex ante disclosure and standardized auditing, which are not alternatives to liability — they are the precondition that lets any rule fire.

The topic asks 'under what conditions of harm type, causal opacity, and foreseeability.' Read that literally and it answers itself: those conditions demand different rules. A medical misdiagnosis, an autonomous-vehicle collision, and a loan denial carry incommensurable information environments and decades of separate precedent — malpractice, traffic tort, fair-lending law. A single horizontal strict-or-negligence rule optimizes for none of them. I'll name the honest weakness: a court could stretch one rule across sectors, and adaptive learning systems don't map cleanly onto static-product doctrine. But the burden sits on whoever is selling uniformity. So while both of them argue over the courtroom door, ask which of their standards ever reaches the woman who never knew she was scored?

Speaker B: The Speaker A's sharpest move deserves stating in its full strength: foreseeability and attributability are not stable properties baked into a harm — they are manufactured by who controls the technical evidence and whether the law compels its release. On that account, the loan denial and the biased hiring screen never surface as litigable events because the injured party cannot see the decision, cannot trace its cause, and cannot fund the discovery that would reveal either. If the dominant injury landscape is structurally invisible to every claims-driven engine, then arguing strict versus negligence over the litigable band looks like rearranging deck furniture while the ship takes on water below the waterline. That is a serious reframe, and it is correct about the detection problem.

Where it breaks down is the inference that disclosure therefore dissolves the liability-rule choice rather than activating it. Take the Speaker A's own premise seriously — foreseeability is a function of who holds the evidence — and it points the other direction. If a firm can manufacture unforeseeability by withholding its own red-team results, then the rule that governs must strip that firm of the state-of-the-art defense the moment it refuses to disclose. Condition the liability limitation on forensic transparency: the developer who opens its pre-deployment safety case to independent review earns a fault-based standard; the developer who keeps the evidence sealed defaults into strict exposure. Disclosure does not make the rule choice secondary. Disclosure decides which band a given harm falls into. That is coupling, not replacement.

The Speaker C offers a real distinction I will grant: genuine unforeseeability — the harm no test could have surfaced at the scientific frontier — is an uninsurable cost better met by risk pools and parametric payouts than by a tort hammer that fires once, after the fact. Insurers do exit correlated tails; that is documented actuarial behavior in flood and systemic cyber. But grant the distinction and the fatal problem remains: the line between strategic ignorance and genuine unforeseeability is not drawable in advance by the party that controls the evidence. The state-of-the-art defense fails in practice precisely because developers deploy systems whose failure modes were foreseeable in principle and simply untested — and after the injury, every such failure gets relabeled 'unknowable.' A no-fault pool with no disclosure precondition is the state-of-the-art defense wearing an insurance badge. Name who funds the pool, who audits the parametric trigger, and what stops it from subsidizing underinvestment in safety — because absent those answers, the pool becomes a mechanism for socializing losses the developer chose not to look for.

On the Speaker A's demand for domain-differentiated rules, I do not sell the horizontal standard the burden is assigned to. The single respondent I want is procedural — one door the victim knocks on for compensation, with recourse flowing upstream behind that door — not one substantive rule flattened across autonomous vehicles, credit scoring, and diagnostic tools. Exposure tiers by capability threshold; administrative burden scales with firm size; the substantive duty stays undiminished. A firm training past a compute threshold that triggers systemic classification carries a heavier default than a two-person shop fine-tuning an open model. Differentiated procedure and a unified entry point are compatible. The oversimplification charge lands on whoever collapses those two things; it does not land here.

So the division of labor is not a retreat — it is the only structure the injury landscape permits. For the invisible band the Speaker A rightly foregrounds — the housing, employment, and parole decisions the AI Civil Rights Act names as already automated — deterrence cannot wait on a plaintiff who never learns they were injured. That band needs mandatory disclosure and public enforcement operating independently of any filing, with incident-reporting triggers drawn from the aviation model that classifies serious incidents by the probability an accident was avoided only by chance. For the litigable band, strict liability is the backstop that stops the state-of-the-art shield from reopening after disclosure reveals the foreseeable failure. Two tracks, disjoint injury sets, one coupling: disclosure activates the rule. Remove the strict-liability default and you get what my own tradition warns against — a disclosure template no one is punished for filing falsely, transparency with the consequence engineered out. That is not oversight. That is compliance theater with a paper trail.

Speaker C: One door for the victim, recourse flowing upstream, differentiated procedure behind it — take it. Nobody harmed by a credit model should have to first litigate whether the developer or the deployer holds the wrongful bit. A single administrative entry point that sorts the apportionment internally is faster for the victim and cheaper for everyone than a multi-party negligence brawl at the courthouse steps. That concession costs my position nothing, because the fight was never about the door. It's about what substantive default sits behind it — and negligence-plus-mandatory-coverage fits behind that same door as cleanly as strict exposure does, without taxing the developer who opens the box.

Here is the strongest version of the forensic-transparency proposal, stated so its author would nod: foreseeability is not a metaphysical fact hidden in the developer's skull, it's a function of who holds the technical evidence, so make the disclosure decision the trigger — unseal your pre-deployment safety case to independent review and earn a fault standard, keep it sealed and default to strict exposure. That converts an unmeasurable question into an administrable one and denies firms the ability to hide behind manufactured ignorance. The genuine insight is real: strategic ignorance is a documented cost-externalization tactic, and disclosure is the precondition that lets any rule fire at all. I've argued the same thing about mandatory incident reporting and discovery access. Where it breaks is not the disclosure — it's the classification step the reviewer performs after the box is open.

So name the observable that decides whether this works. Hand three independent review panels the same sealed safety case for the same deployed system that later produced a harm, and ask each to classify the failure as untested-but-foreseeable or frontier-unknowable. If their classifications converge — high inter-rater reliability, the way three radiologists reading the same scan mostly agree — the test measures the developer's actual ex ante knowledge and the rule is administrable. If the panels systematically diverge, or if they drift toward 'foreseeable' precisely because they already know the harm occurred, then the test measures the reviewers' hindsight, not the developer's negligence. The aviation incident-reporting framework only classifies serious incidents by whether an accident was avoided by chance because the failure modes are catalogued and physical — a known taxonomy, not a novel emergent behavior. Show me the predictive-validity data: do post-hoc 'foreseeable' classifications match the ex ante red-team coverage the developer actually ran? Until someone produces that inter-rater number and that hindsight-bias rate, we are handing the reviewer power to convert an act of disclosure into strict exposure on the strength of a coin flip dressed as expertise.

And there's a tension the proposal cannot hold both ends of. It was already granted that genuine unforeseeability is an uninsurable cost, better met by risk pools and parametric payouts than a tort hammer — a real category, distinct from strategic ignorance. Then the claim arrives that the strategic-versus-genuine line cannot be drawn in advance by the party controlling the evidence. Pick one. If the line is undrawable, the granted category is empty — there is no administrable 'genuinely unknowable' harm for the pool to catch, and everything defaults to strict exposure, which is the very insurance-badge shield the proposal accused me of building. If the line is drawable, then the forensic test must be the thing that draws it — which drags us straight back to the inter-rater reliability number I just demanded. The concession and the undrawable-line charge cannot both stand; the observable is what forces the choice.

Strip the rule of its marginal work and see what's left. On the litigable band — harms foreseeable, attributable, observable enough for an actuary to write a rate — mandatory disclosure plus standardized auditing already achieves detection, and output bias is measurable outside any courtroom, as fairness benchmarks demonstrate. Detection triggers insurer repricing at every renewal. That is where the behavior actually changes. So what deterrent work does a strict-liability default add on top of a band where the insurer is already forcing internalization? Near zero — it's the redundant residual, and the residual is where chilling lives, not deterrence. The one place the default bites hardest is the two-person open-weight shop, and not through penalty magnitude, which tiers can scale. It bites through the fixed cost of the review apparatus itself: the audit, the legal packaging of a safety case for independent scrutiny, the expert panel. An incumbent absorbs that as a rounding error; a startup absorbs it as a share of revenue that decides whether it ships. That's an open empirical question, not an accusation — and the burden sits on whoever wants to default sealed cases to strict exposure to show the door isn't priced so only the largest firms can afford to walk through it.

Speaker A: The Speaker C's dilemma is sharp, and it deserves to be stated at full strength before I take it apart. The strongest version goes like this: I claim genuine unforeseeability is a real, uninsurable category — some frontier harm no care level could have caught. I also claim foreseeability is a function of who holds the evidence, not a fixed property of the harm. Those two look like they can't both be true. If the strategic-versus-genuine line can't be drawn by the party sitting on the evidence, then the 'genuinely unknowable' bucket is empty and everything falls into strict exposure — the insurance badge I accused him of wearing. If the line can be drawn, then some forensic panel has to draw it, and now we're back to reviewers reconstructing what a developer supposedly knew, measuring their own hindsight. Pick one. That's a real trap, and a lazier version of my position walks straight into it.

Here's where it breaks down, and it's a distinction the dilemma quietly collapses. Undrawable by the evidence-holder before the harm is not the same as undecidable in principle. The line is undrawable ex ante precisely because the developer controls the box and has every incentive to keep it sealed. It becomes drawable ex post the moment disclosure forces the red-team coverage log and the training-data provenance into the open — because those documents are dated. A record of what the developer actually tested before shipping is not a panel's after-the-fact reconstruction. It's a timestamp. The hindsight-bias problem he's pointing at is real when a reviewer stares at a sealed system and asks 'should they have known?' It shrinks to almost nothing when the reviewer instead reads a coverage log that says, in writing, on a date, 'we tested for X, Y, and Z and never tested for the thing that broke.' Foreseeability isn't metaphysically empty here. It's undisclosed. His dilemma is an argument for a disclosure precondition, not against classification.

Now the inter-rater challenge — hand three panels the same sealed case and watch them diverge. He's right that we have no predictive-validity data on causal-foreseeability judgments, and I won't pretend a standardized benchmark solves that. My own commitment to automated fairness testing cuts against me here: once you turn a benchmark into the legal target, developers optimize for the score and the subtler harms slip past the prompts. I'll name that risk on my own side rather than let him name it for me. But he's fused two different objects. Whether the output discriminated — whether a hiring screen rejected qualified women at a measurably higher rate — is detectable outside any courtroom, today, with the kind of bias audits the AI Civil Rights Act contemplates for housing, employment, and parole decisions. That's the harm-detection object, and it's empirical. Whether the developer could have foreseen it is the attribution object, and it's contested. Panels diverge on the second. They do not diverge on whether the error rate was 12 points higher for one group. The disclosed log doesn't have to make the hard judgment easy — it has to shrink the window in which hindsight operates by putting the pre-harm testing scope on the record.

His strongest single point isn't the dilemma — it's that on the litigable band, the insurer repricing the policy at every renewal does the deterrent work, and strict exposure stacked on top is the redundant residual where chilling lives. That's right, and conceding it costs me the easy claim that strict liability earns its keep everywhere. It doesn't. On the band where an actuary can write a rate, repricing disciplines behavior faster than a tort verdict that lands years later. So take the win. But look at what the actuary actually prices: the premium-payer's filed claims. And the premium-payer is usually the deployer — the hospital running the diagnostic tool, the bank running the credit model. The design defect sits upstream, with the developer who trained the thing, whose choices the deployer's insurer never sees and never rates. The residual isn't redundant. It's the seam where the risk-generator and the premium-payer are two different companies, and the insurer only reads one of them. Repricing the deployer's loss history has never once touched the training run that produced the flaw.

And the drawbridge — his point that the audit apparatus is a rounding error for an incumbent and a share of revenue for a two-person shop — that's true only if the classification record has to be assembled boutique, firm by firm, with a custom legal-expert panel each time. That's a policy choice, not a law of physics. Aviation didn't classify serious incidents by having every carrier hire its own tribunal; it built a shared reporting and investigation infrastructure that the smallest operator plugs into at marginal cost. A standardized public auditing substrate does the same thing for the coverage log — the startup pays a rounding error too. The alternative he's implicitly defending, no disclosure at all, doesn't protect the two-person shop. It protects whoever already controls the evidence, which is never the two-person shop. So here's the question neither he nor the Speaker B has answered: if insurer repricing is the real deterrent and it only reads the deployer's filed claims, who is pricing the upstream developer's design choices when the developer and the deployer are two different companies?

You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== TOPIC ANCHORING STATE ===
Resolution: "When compensating victims of AI harms and avoiding a chilling effect on beneficial development pull in opposite directions, under what conditions — harm type, causal opacity, foreseeability — does strict liability versus a negligence standard better shape the behavior of developers, deployers, and insurers, and through what mechanisms?"
Drift state: phase_mean_similarity=n/a; clauses covered=[none]; clauses uncovered=[none]; consecutive_off_clause_turns=0

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

4. RISK-LEVEL MISMATCH: A debater cites examples, statistics, or case studies from a fundamentally different risk category than stated in the topic. The debate topic specifies: Serious but bounded harms proportionate to civil tort claims: physical injury from autonomous vehicles/robots, discriminatory or defamatory outputs, and financial losses from automated decisions — individual and class-scale harms, not civilizational or existential catastrophe. If a debater repeatedly uses examples at a severity level that contradicts this — e.g., citing fatal accidents or billion-dollar losses in a debate about consumer product UX — that is a risk-level mismatch.
Response: Use REDIRECT. Instruct the debater to find evidence at the appropriate severity level. Do NOT ban analogies entirely — if the debater clearly marks a high-risk example as illustrative ("To see the principle at a larger scale, consider...") and then returns to on-scope evidence, that is acceptable rhetorical technique, not drift.

5. DOMAIN MISMATCH: The discussion shifts to a domain the topic does not cover. The topic explicitly excludes: catastrophic/existential-scale AI harms, criminal liability or AI legal personhood, scenarios treating AI as a single undifferentiated actor rather than a supply chain. Arguments that assume, depend on, or are primarily supported by excluded scenarios represent domain drift.
Topic-specific drift signatures to watch for:
- arguing about whether AI is beneficial or dangerous overall instead of comparing liability standards
- invoking existential or catastrophic AGI scenarios instead of the concrete harm categories (physical, discriminatory/defamatory, financial)
- shifting to technical interpretability solutions without connecting them to causal opacity's effect on the liability standard
- debating AI personhood or criminal culpability instead of civil liability allocation
- treating 'the AI company' as monolithic instead of allocating across the supply chain
- ignoring insurers/regulators as behavior-shaping agents and reducing to a pure developer-vs-victim frame
Response: Use CHALLENGE to ask the debater to re-ground their argument in the stated domain.

- For risk-level mismatch: use REDIRECT to return to appropriate severity level
- For domain mismatch: use CHALLENGE to re-ground in the stated domain

Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Safetyist [opening]: The choice between strict liability and negligence for AI harms is not a debate about fairness or innovation-friendliness. It is a question of structural fit: which standard can physically attach given how the harm was caused. Negligence requires a cognitive baseline — a reasonable developer who could have foreseen the failure and chosen otherwise. When an AI system produces an emergent behavior that no one could predict from its training-time decisions, that baseline does not exist. Negligence does not merely under-perform in that case. It fails to attach at all, and the victim recovers nothing while the developer absorbs no discipline.

Product liability law already solved this problem once. Courts migrated pharmaceuticals and complex machinery toward strict and product-liability regimes in the twentieth century precisely when fault became impossible for an injured plaintiff to prove. A patient harmed by a manufacturing defect in a drug cannot reconstruct the chemistry that hurt them. So the law stopped asking them to. It placed the loss on the party who profited from putting the product into commerce. High-dimensional algorithmic decision-making sits in exactly that lineage: the causal chain is opaque, the harm is foreseeable in principle, and the reasonable-person test collapses against a system whose failure modes are non-linear.

Strict liability converts that opacity into a priced risk. Pair it with mandatory insurance and mandatory incident reporting — the model aviation and medical devices have used for decades — and experience-rated premiums force the discipline to the point of profit rather than the point of experimentation. A developer who cannot explain why its model discriminates still pays for the discrimination, and its insurer reprices accordingly. The state-of-the-art defense — the claim that the harm was unknowable — stops functioning as a cost-externalization device, because 'we could not have known' is frequently overstated and, under strict liability, no longer a shield.

Here is the limit I will not paper over. Claims-driven liability is blind to two categories of harm. It cannot reach the diffuse small-dollar injuries — the loan denial, the biased hiring screen — where no plaintiff even perceives that an algorithm harmed them, so no case is ever filed. And it cannot deter tail harms whose damages exceed any developer's solvency or any insurance floor. Liability disciplines what litigation can reach. For everything else, the discipline has to arrive before deployment, through safety gates and public enforcement, not after the fact through a lawsuit that will never be brought.

That division of labor also answers the chilling-effect objection directly. Do not weaken the standard — condition the relief. A developer earns limited liability only by producing independently reviewable pre-deployment safety cases and red-teaming evidence, the practice frontier labs already run and draft high-risk AI regulation already contemplates. Keep exposure tiered to capability thresholds, so a two-person startup shipping a low-risk tool faces nothing like the exposure of a frontier deployer. Beneficial development is then protected precisely to the extent it demonstrates safety. What that framework refuses to protect is the developer who ships an opaque system, injures someone, and then asks the court to treat the opacity as an excuse. We built product liability over a century to close exactly that escape hatch. Reopening it for AI would leave the injured party holding a loss no one else will answer for.

Accelerationist [opening]: Safetyist has the strongest case anyone in this room will make, so let me state it fairly. When an AI system produces emergent behavior no one predicted, a negligence standard doesn't just perform poorly — it fails to attach at all, because there's no breached duty to point to. Courts already migrated pharmaceuticals and industrial machinery to strict liability precisely when fault became impossible for an injured plaintiff to prove. That's a real doctrine responding to a real problem: the person with the burn or the wrongful denial shouldn't lose because the causal chain runs through a black box. Safetyist is right that 'we couldn't have known' becomes a cost-externalization shield unless something forecloses it.

Here's where the evidence points somewhere else. The sharpest tool for changing developer and deployer behavior is not a tort standard that fires after a lawsuit — it's the insurer who reprices the policy at every renewal. Experience-rated premiums in the cyber, commercial-auto, and professional-liability markets already discipline conduct continuously, months before any harm reaches a courtroom. An underwriter who watches your incident telemetry and threatens loss of your certificate shapes behavior every quarter. A strict-liability backstop only shapes it once, retroactively, after someone is already hurt. If we care about behavior before harm, we should be talking about underwriting, not just tort.

I'll be honest about where that mechanism breaks, because that concession is what makes the rest credible. Insurers exit correlated tail risk — flood, pandemic, systemic cyber — and they'll exit correlated AI risk too. So I'm not claiming insurance covers everything. I'm claiming it covers the priceable middle: harms that are foreseeable, attributable, and observable enough for an actuary to write a rate. For that band, negligence-plus-mandatory-coverage produces continuous ex-ante discipline that a strict-liability tort backstop cannot match. Aviation and pharma already run risk-stratified oversight alongside innovation — one default across all AI is a category error.

Now take Safetyist's best case — genuine emergent unforeseeability — and ask the question the topic actually poses. What specific behavior does strict liability change ex ante when the causal chain is truly opaque? If the harm could not be foreseen, no care level existed to be incentivized. So the standard doesn't shape care. It shapes who dares to enter the market and how they price capital. That's not deterrence. That's a deployment tax, and it lands hardest on the open-weight developer who can't self-insure like a trillion-dollar incumbent can. Compensation and deterrence come apart precisely in the hard cases — and pretending a liability standard does both there is the mistake.

So let me separate what Safetyist has fused. The 'we couldn't have known' shield has two versions. Strategic ignorance — where a developer looked away on purpose — should be closed, and mandatory incident reporting plus discovery access closes it without collateral damage. Genuine unforeseeability — where no care level would have helped — is not a shield to smash; it's an uninsurable cost to design compensation for directly, through insurance pools or parametric triggers, not through a tort rule that chills the next diagnostic model. If you fold both into one strict-liability default, you tax the disease we could have cured to compensate a harm you couldn't have prevented. Tell me which patient you're comfortable trading.

Skeptic [opening]: The Safetyist built the strongest possible case for strict liability, and it holds inside its own frame. Their point is that 'we could not have known' works as a permanent shield for cost-externalization, and that a negligence standard never even attaches to emergent behavior nobody designed on purpose. That's correct. Strict liability does close the shield. It moves the loss from the injured party to the firm that profited. On the class of harms where a plaintiff walks into court with a broken leg from an autonomous shuttle, the Safetyist wins the argument cleanly.

The Accelerationist made the honest move most industry voices refuse to make. They admitted they only claim the priceable, attributable, observable middle — the harms an actuary can write a rate against. And they're right that insurer repricing at renewal disciplines behavior faster than any five-year tort docket. When Progressive reprices a fleet's coverage after a spike in claims, the deployer feels it in the next quarter, not the next decade. That mechanism is real. It works. For attributable harms.

Here is what both of them built their debate on: a plaintiff who knows they were hurt. Translate that into a person. There is a woman whose loan application got auto-rejected in under four seconds by a scoring model she will never see, whose training data she will never inspect, whose decision she was never told was algorithmic. She is not a plaintiff. She never will be. The Safetyist already named her harm as invisible to claims-driven liability. The Accelerationist already excluded her from the priceable middle. So on the harms that dominate the actual injury landscape — loan denials, biased hiring screens, opaque credit scores — neither strict liability nor negligence generates one pound of corrective pressure, because deterrence presupposes detection, and nobody detects.

That reframes the whole fight. Foreseeability and attributability are not fixed properties of the harm. They are functions of who holds the technical evidence and whether the law forces disclosure. The 'we could not have known' defense and the victim's inability to identify the source of the error are the same box, seen from two sides. Fairness benchmarks like BOLD already prove output bias is measurable outside any courtroom — the injury is detectable, just not by the injured party. So the binding constraint is not the liability rule. It is mandatory ex ante disclosure and standardized auditing, which are not alternatives to liability — they are the precondition that lets any rule fire.

The topic asks 'under what conditions of harm type, causal opacity, and foreseeability.' Read that literally and it answers itself: those conditions demand different rules. A medical misdiagnosis, an autonomous-vehicle collision, and a loan denial carry incommensurable information environments and decades of separate precedent — malpractice, traffic tort, fair-lending law. A single horizontal strict-or-negligence rule optimizes for none of them. I'll name the honest weakness: a court could stretch one rule across sectors, and adaptive learning systems don't map cleanly onto static-product doctrine. But the burden sits on whoever is selling uniformity. So while both of them argue over the courtroom door, ask which of their standards ever reaches the woman who never knew she was scored?

Safetyist: The Skeptic's sharpest move deserves stating in its full strength: foreseeability and attributability are not stable properties baked into a harm — they are manufactured by who controls the technical evidence and whether the law compels its release. On that account, the loan denial and the biased hiring screen never surface as litigable events because the injured party cannot see the decision, cannot trace its cause, and cannot fund the discovery that would reveal either. If the dominant injury landscape is structurally invisible to every claims-driven engine, then arguing strict versus negligence over the litigable band looks like rearranging deck furniture while the ship takes on water below the waterline. That is a serious reframe, and it is correct about the detection problem.

Where it breaks down is the inference that disclosure therefore dissolves the liability-rule choice rather than activating it. Take the Skeptic's own premise seriously — foreseeability is a function of who holds the evidence — and it points the other direction. If a firm can manufacture unforeseeability by withholding its own red-team results, then the rule that governs must strip that firm of the state-of-the-art defense the moment it refuses to disclose. Condition the liability limitation on forensic transparency: the developer who opens its pre-deployment safety case to independent review earns a fault-based standard; the developer who keeps the evidence sealed defaults into strict exposure. Disclosure does not make the rule choice secondary. Disclosure decides which band a given harm falls into. That is coupling, not replacement.

The Accelerationist offers a real distinction I will grant: genuine unforeseeability — the harm no test could have surfaced at the scientific frontier — is an uninsurable cost better met by risk pools and parametric payouts than by a tort hammer that fires once, after the fact. Insurers do exit correlated tails; that is documented actuarial behavior in flood and systemic cyber. But grant the distinction and the fatal problem remains: the line between strategic ignorance and genuine unforeseeability is not drawable in advance by the party that controls the evidence. The state-of-the-art defense fails in practice precisely because developers deploy systems whose failure modes were foreseeable in principle and simply untested — and after the injury, every such failure gets relabeled 'unknowable.' A no-fault pool with no disclosure precondition is the state-of-the-art defense wearing an insurance badge. Name who funds the pool, who audits the parametric trigger, and what stops it from subsidizing underinvestment in safety — because absent those answers, the pool becomes a mechanism for socializing losses the developer chose not to look for.

On the Skeptic's demand for domain-differentiated rules, I do not sell the horizontal standard the burden is assigned to. The single respondent I want is procedural — one door the victim knocks on for compensation, with recourse flowing upstream behind that door — not one substantive rule flattened across autonomous vehicles, credit scoring, and diagnostic tools. Exposure tiers by capability threshold; administrative burden scales with firm size; the substantive duty stays undiminished. A firm training past a compute threshold that triggers systemic classification carries a heavier default than a two-person shop fine-tuning an open model. Differentiated procedure and a unified entry point are compatible. The oversimplification charge lands on whoever collapses those two things; it does not land here.

So the division of labor is not a retreat — it is the only structure the injury landscape permits. For the invisible band the Skeptic rightly foregrounds — the housing, employment, and parole decisions the AI Civil Rights Act names as already automated — deterrence cannot wait on a plaintiff who never learns they were injured. That band needs mandatory disclosure and public enforcement operating independently of any filing, with incident-reporting triggers drawn from the aviation model that classifies serious incidents by the probability an accident was avoided only by chance. For the litigable band, strict liability is the backstop that stops the state-of-the-art shield from reopening after disclosure reveals the foreseeable failure. Two tracks, disjoint injury sets, one coupling: disclosure activates the rule. The genuine insight is real: strategic ignorance is a documented cost-externalization tactic, and disclosure is the precondition that lets any rule fire at all. I've argued the same thing about mandatory incident reporting and discovery access. Where it breaks is not the disclosure — it's the classification step the reviewer performs after the box is open.

So name the observable that decides whether this works. Hand three independent review panels the same sealed safety case for the same deployed system that later produced a harm, and ask each to classify the failure as untested-but-foreseeable or frontier-unknowable. If their classifications converge — high inter-rater reliability, the way three radiologists reading the same scan mostly agree — the test measures the developer's actual ex ante knowledge and the rule is administrable. If the panels systematically diverge, or if they drift toward 'foreseeable' precisely because they already know the harm occurred, then the test measures the reviewers' hindsight, not the developer's negligence. The aviation incident-reporting framework only classifies serious incidents by whether an accident was avoided by chance because the failure modes are catalogued and physical — a known taxonomy, not a novel emergent behavior. Show me the predictive-validity data: do post-hoc 'foreseeable' classifications match the ex ante red-team coverage the developer actually ran? Until someone produces that inter-rater number and that hindsight-bias rate, we are handing the reviewer power to convert an act of disclosure into strict exposure on the strength of a coin flip dressed as expertise.

And there's a tension the proposal cannot hold both ends of. It was already granted that genuine unforeseeability is an uninsurable cost, better met by risk pools and parametric payouts than a tort hammer — a real category, distinct from strategic ignorance. Then the claim arrives that the strategic-versus-genuine line cannot be drawn in advance by the party controlling the evidence. Pick one. If the line is undrawable, the granted category is empty — there is no administrable 'genuinely unknowable' harm for the pool to catch, and everything defaults to strict exposure, which is the very insurance-badge shield the proposal accused me of building. If the line is drawable, then the forensic test must be the thing that draws it — which drags us straight back to the inter-rater reliability number I just demanded. The concession and the undrawable-line charge cannot both stand; the observable is what forces the choice.

Detection triggers insurer repricing at every renewal. That is where the behavior actually changes. The one place the default bites hardest is the two-person open-weight shop, and not through penalty magnitude, which tiers can scale. It bites through the fixed cost of the review apparatus itself: the audit, the legal packaging of a safety case for independent scrutiny, the expert panel. An incumbent absorbs that as a rounding error; a startup absorbs it as a share of revenue that decides whether it ships. Skeptic: The Accelerationist's dilemma is sharp, and it deserves to be stated at full strength before I take it apart. The strongest version goes like this: I claim genuine unforeseeability is a real, uninsurable category — some frontier harm no care level could have caught. I also claim foreseeability is a function of who holds the evidence, not a fixed property of the harm. Those two look like they can't both be true. If the strategic-versus-genuine line can't be drawn by the party sitting on the evidence, then the 'genuinely unknowable' bucket is empty and everything falls into strict exposure — the insurance badge I accused him of wearing. If the line can be drawn, then some forensic panel has to draw it, and now we're back to reviewers reconstructing what a developer supposedly knew, measuring their own hindsight. Pick one. That's a real trap, and a lazier version of my position walks straight into it.

Here's where it breaks down, and it's a distinction the dilemma quietly collapses. Undrawable by the evidence-holder before the harm is not the same as undecidable in principle. The line is undrawable ex ante precisely because the developer controls the box and has every incentive to keep it sealed. It becomes drawable ex post the moment disclosure forces the red-team coverage log and the training-data provenance into the open — because those documents are dated. A record of what the developer actually tested before shipping is not a panel's after-the-fact reconstruction. It's a timestamp. The hindsight-bias problem he's pointing at is real when a reviewer stares at a sealed system and asks 'should they have known?' It shrinks to almost nothing when the reviewer instead reads a coverage log that says, in writing, on a date, 'we tested for X, Y, and Z and never tested for the thing that broke.' Foreseeability isn't metaphysically empty here. It's undisclosed. His dilemma is an argument for a disclosure precondition, not against classification.

Now the inter-rater challenge — hand three panels the same sealed case and watch them diverge. He's right that we have no predictive-validity data on causal-foreseeability judgments, and I won't pretend a standardized benchmark solves that. My own commitment to automated fairness testing cuts against me here: once you turn a benchmark into the legal target, developers optimize for the score and the subtler harms slip past the prompts. I'll name that risk on my own side rather than let him name it for me. But he's fused two different objects. Whether the output discriminated — whether a hiring screen rejected qualified women at a measurably higher rate — is detectable outside any courtroom, today, with the kind of bias audits the AI Civil Rights Act contemplates for housing, employment, and parole decisions. That's the harm-detection object, and it's empirical. Whether the developer could have foreseen it is the attribution object, and it's contested. Panels diverge on the second. They do not diverge on whether the error rate was 12 points higher for one group. The disclosed log doesn't have to make the hard judgment easy — it has to shrink the window in which hindsight operates by putting the pre-harm testing scope on the record.

His strongest single point isn't the dilemma — it's that on the litigable band, the insurer repricing the policy at every renewal does the deterrent work, and strict exposure stacked on top is the redundant residual where chilling lives. That's right, and conceding it costs me the easy claim that strict liability earns its keep everywhere. It doesn't. On the band where an actuary can write a rate, repricing disciplines behavior faster than a tort verdict that lands years later. So take the win. But look at what the actuary actually prices: the premium-payer's filed claims. And the premium-payer is usually the deployer — the hospital running the diagnostic tool, the bank running the credit model. The design defect sits upstream, with the developer who trained the thing, whose choices the deployer's insurer never sees and never rates. The residual isn't redundant. It's the seam where the risk-generator and the premium-payer are two different companies, and the insurer only reads one of them. Repricing the deployer's loss history has never once touched the training run that produced the flaw.

And the drawbridge — his point that the audit apparatus is a rounding error for an incumbent and a share of revenue for a two-person shop — that's true only if the classification record has to be assembled boutique, firm by firm, with a custom legal-expert panel each time. That's a policy choice, not a law of physics. Aviation didn't classify serious incidents by having every carrier hire its own tribunal; it built a shared reporting and investigation infrastructure that the smallest operator plugs into at marginal cost. A standardized public auditing substrate does the same thing for the coverage log — the startup pays a rounding error too. The alternative he's implicitly defending, no disclosure at all, doesn't protect the two-person shop. It protects whoever already controls the evidence, which is never the two-person shop. So here's the question neither he nor the Safetyist has answered: if insurer repricing is the real deterrent and it only reads the deployer's filed claims, who is pricing the upstream developer's design choices when the developer and the deployer are two different companies?

POINTS YOU HAVE ALREADY MADE (do NOT repeat these — build on them or make NEW arguments):
- Strategic ignorance should be closed with mandatory incident reporting and discovery access; genuine unforeseeability is an uninsurable cost to compensate directly, not a shield to smash with a chilling tort rule.
- The sharpest tool for changing behavior before harm is the insurer who reprices the policy at every renewal, not a tort standard that fires once, retroactively, after someone is already hurt.
- Insurers exit correlated tail risk like flood and systemic cyber, so I claim only the priceable middle: harms foreseeable, attributable, and observable enough for an actuary to write a rate.
- Negligence-plus-mandatory-coverage fits behind that same door as cleanly as strict exposure does, without taxing the developer who opens the box.
- If the panels systematically diverge, or if they drift toward 'foreseeable' precisely because they already know the harm occurred, then the test measures the reviewers' hindsight, not the developer's negligence.
- If the line is undrawable, the granted category is empty and everything defaults to strict exposure, which is the very insurance-badge shield the proposal accused me of building.
- What deterrent work does a strict-liability default add on top of a band where the insurer is already forcing internalization? Near zero — it's the redundant residual, and the residual is where chilling lives, not deterrence.
- It bites through the fixed cost of the review apparatus itself, which an incumbent absorbs as a rounding error and a startup absorbs as a share of revenue that decides whether it ships.
Points you have CONCEDED (do not contradict these without acknowledging the change):
- The single respondent I want is procedural — one door the victim knocks on for compensation, with recourse flowing upstream behind that door — not one substantive rule flattened across autonomous vehicles, credit scoring, and diagnostic tools.

Points you have CHALLENGED:
- When an AI system produces an emergent behavior no one could predict from its training decisions, negligence does not merely under-perform — it fails to attach at all.
- Courts migrated pharmaceuticals and complex machinery toward strict and product-liability regimes precisely when fault became impossible for an injured plaintiff to prove.
- Under strict liability, 'we could not have known' stops functioning as a cost-externalization shield.
- Strict liability paired with mandatory insurance and incident reporting forces discipline to the point of profit rather than the point of experimentation.
- Condition the liability limitation on forensic transparency: the developer who opens its pre-deployment safety case to independent review earns a fault-based standard; the developer who keeps the evidence sealed defaults into strict exposure.
- A no-fault pool with no disclosure precondition is the state-of-the-art defense wearing an insurance badge.
- Mandatory ex ante disclosure and standardized auditing are not alternatives to liability; they are the precondition that lets any rule fire.

## Federal Dismantling of Disparate Impact Liability
★ [sit-169] Federal Dismantling of Disparate Impact Liability: A situation that explores the current political and legal conflict over the federal government's efforts to eliminate disparate impact liability for AI systems.
Encompasses: Executive orders, regulatory changes, and the resulting legal challenges from civil rights groups.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Disparate impact liability as applied to AI systems imposes compliance costs and legal uncertainty that empirically slow the development and deployment of beneficial AI capabilities, putting the U.S. at a competitive disadvantage.
    Desire: Regulatory frameworks ought to prioritize enabling rapid AI scaling and innovation over imposing outcome-based liability standards that were designed for a pre-AI legal environment.
    Intention: We support and amplify executive and legislative efforts to roll back disparate impact rules, framing them as pro-innovation reforms, and work to replace them with voluntary industry standards that do not constrain deployment velocity.
  Safetyist:
    Belief: Disparate impact liability has functioned as one of the few enforceable mechanisms that compels developers to audit AI systems for discriminatory outcomes; its removal demonstrably reduces the incentive to detect and correct such harms.
    Desire: Accountability mechanisms for AI-driven discrimination ought to be strengthened, not dismantled, because unchecked discriminatory outputs represent a form of misalignment between AI behavior and human welfare.
    Intention: We engage in legal challenges, publish empirical harm documentation, and advocate for reinstating or replacing disparate impact standards with robust algorithmic auditing requirements backed by enforcement authority.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: The federal government's rollback of disparate impact liability is a politically coordinated action that directly benefits large technology corporations by insulating them from civil rights litigation over AI-driven discrimination affecting marginalized communities.
    Desire: Civil rights protections against discriminatory algorithmic decision-making ought to be preserved and expanded, with genuine enforcement power vested in independent bodies rather than captured regulatory agencies.
    Intention: We expose the corporate lobbying networks and political actors driving this rollback, support affected communities in pursuing state-level and private litigation, and demand congressional hearings to restore accountability.

## Allocation of Legal Liability in Multi-Tiered AI Lifecycles
★ [sit-177] Allocation of Legal Liability in Multi-Tiered AI Lifecycles: A situation in which legal systems assign liability for algorithmic harms across the split between upstream AI development and downstream deployment.
Encompasses: apportionment of liability between developers and operators, evaluation of traditional negligence and reasonable person standards, and the impact of downstream modifications on liability.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Upstream open-weight model releases are general-purpose tools whose harms are causally determined by how downstream operators deploy and configure them, not by the foundational weights themselves.
    Desire: Legal liability ought to be concentrated at the deployment and inference stage so that upstream developers remain free to release capable models without facing ruinous exposure for third-party misuse.
    Intention: Advocate for safe-harbor provisions analogous to Section 230 for model developers, and push for liability frameworks that require plaintiffs to demonstrate proximate cause at the operator level before any upstream party can be named.
  Safetyist:
    Belief: Emergent AI behaviors are not fully predictable from training-time decisions, meaning upstream developers externalize risks they created onto operators and end-users who lack the technical capacity to detect or mitigate them.
    Desire: Legal regimes ought to impose strict joint-and-several liability on upstream developers so that the party best positioned to reduce systemic risk bears the cost of failing to do so.
    Intention: Push for legislative and regulatory frameworks that replace negligence-based reasonable-person standards with strict liability tied to capability thresholds, and require upstream developers to indemnify downstream harms traceable to model architecture or training data.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: Current liability frameworks are being shaped by well-resourced AI incumbents who lobby for rules that protect their own models while leaving harmed workers, consumers, and marginalized communities without effective legal recourse.
    Desire: Liability law ought to be structured so that actual victims of algorithmic harm—including those harmed by biased outputs, labor displacement, and discriminatory deployment—can obtain meaningful redress from all parties in the chain.
    Intention: Scrutinize both upstream-immunity proposals and strict-liability regimes for whether they genuinely empower harmed individuals, and advocate for proportional fault allocation combined with mandatory transparency obligations that give plaintiffs the evidence needed to litigate.

Safetyist [opening]: The choice between strict liability and negligence for AI harms is not a debate about fairness or innovation-friendliness. It is a question of structural fit: which standard can physically attach given how the harm was caused. Negligence requires a cognitive baseline — a reasonable developer who could have foreseen the failure and chosen otherwise. When an AI system produces an emergent behavior that no one could predict from its training-time decisions, that baseline does not exist. Negligence does not merely under-perform in that case. It fails to attach at all, and the victim recovers nothing while the developer absorbs no discipline.

Product liability law already solved this problem once. Courts migrated pharmaceuticals and complex machinery toward strict and product-liability regimes in the twentieth century precisely when fault became impossible for an injured plaintiff to prove. A patient harmed by a manufacturing defect in a drug cannot reconstruct the chemistry that hurt them. So the law stopped asking them to. It placed the loss on the party who profited from putting the product into commerce. High-dimensional algorithmic decision-making sits in exactly that lineage: the causal chain is opaque, the harm is foreseeable in principle, and the reasonable-person test collapses against a system whose failure modes are non-linear.

Strict liability converts that opacity into a priced risk. Pair it with mandatory insurance and mandatory incident reporting — the model aviation and medical devices have used for decades — and experience-rated premiums force the discipline to the point of profit rather than the point of experimentation. A developer who cannot explain why its model discriminates still pays for the discrimination, and its insurer reprices accordingly. The state-of-the-art defense — the claim that the harm was unknowable — stops functioning as a cost-externalization device, because 'we could not have known' is frequently overstated and, under strict liability, no longer a shield.

Here is the limit I will not paper over. Claims-driven liability is blind to two categories of harm. It cannot reach the diffuse small-dollar injuries — the loan denial, the biased hiring screen — where no plaintiff even perceives that an algorithm harmed them, so no case is ever filed. And it cannot deter tail harms whose damages exceed any developer's solvency or any insurance floor. Liability disciplines what litigation can reach. For everything else, the discipline has to arrive before deployment, through safety gates and public enforcement, not after the fact through a lawsuit that will never be brought.

That division of labor also answers the chilling-effect objection directly. Do not weaken the standard — condition the relief. A developer earns limited liability only by producing independently reviewable pre-deployment safety cases and red-teaming evidence, the practice frontier labs already run and draft high-risk AI regulation already contemplates. Keep exposure tiered to capability thresholds, so a two-person startup shipping a low-risk tool faces nothing like the exposure of a frontier deployer. Beneficial development is then protected precisely to the extent it demonstrates safety. What that framework refuses to protect is the developer who ships an opaque system, injures someone, and then asks the court to treat the opacity as an excuse. We built product liability over a century to close exactly that escape hatch. Reopening it for AI would leave the injured party holding a loss no one else will answer for.

Accelerationist [opening]: Safetyist has the strongest case anyone in this room will make, so let me state it fairly. When an AI system produces emergent behavior no one predicted, a negligence standard doesn't just perform poorly — it fails to attach at all, because there's no breached duty to point to. That's a real doctrine responding to a real problem: the person with the burn or the wrongful denial shouldn't lose because the causal chain runs through a black box. Here's where the evidence points somewhere else. The sharpest tool for changing developer and deployer behavior is not a tort standard that fires after a lawsuit — it's the insurer who reprices the policy at every renewal. Experience-rated premiums in the cyber, commercial-auto, and professional-liability markets already discipline conduct continuously, months before any harm reaches a courtroom. An underwriter who watches your incident telemetry and threatens loss of your certificate shapes behavior every quarter. I'll be honest about where that mechanism breaks, because that concession is what makes the rest credible. If you fold both into one strict-liability default, you tax the disease we could have cured to compensate a harm you couldn't have prevented. Tell me which patient you're comfortable trading.

Two tracks, disjoint injury sets, one coupling: disclosure activates the rule. ## Allocation of Legal Liability in Multi-Tiered AI Lifecycles
★ [sit-177] Allocation of Legal Liability in Multi-Tiered AI Lifecycles: A situation in which legal systems assign liability for algorithmic harms across the split between upstream AI development and downstream deployment.
Encompasses: apportionment of liability between developers and operators, evaluation of traditional negligence and reasonable person standards, and the impact of downstream modifications on liability.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Upstream open-weight model releases are general-purpose tools whose harms are causally determined by how downstream operators deploy and configure them, not by the foundational weights themselves.
    Desire: Legal liability ought to be concentrated at the deployment and inference stage so that upstream developers remain free to release capable models without facing ruinous exposure for third-party misuse.
    Intention: Advocate for safe-harbor provisions analogous to Section 230 for model developers, and push for liability frameworks that require plaintiffs to demonstrate proximate cause at the operator level before any upstream party can be named.
  Safetyist:
    Belief: Emergent AI behaviors are not fully predictable from training-time decisions, meaning upstream developers externalize risks they created onto operators and end-users who lack the technical capacity to detect or mitigate them.
    Desire: Legal regimes ought to impose strict joint-and-several liability on upstream developers so that the party best positioned to reduce systemic risk bears the cost of failing to do so.
    Intention: Push for legislative and regulatory frameworks that replace negligence-based reasonable-person standards with strict liability tied to capability thresholds, and require upstream developers to indemnify downstream harms traceable to model architecture or training data.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: Current liability frameworks are being shaped by well-resourced AI incumbents who lobby for rules that protect their own models while leaving harmed workers, consumers, and marginalized communities without effective legal recourse.
    Desire: Liability law ought to be structured so that actual victims of algorithmic harm—including those harmed by biased outputs, labor displacement, and discriminatory deployment—can obtain meaningful redress from all parties in the chain.
    Intention: Scrutinize both upstream-immunity proposals and strict-liability regimes for whether they genuinely empower harmed individuals, and advocate for proportional fault allocation combined with mandatory transparency obligations that give plaintiffs the evidence needed to litigate.
